sentences.text: But of course, that's just a description, too, that's layered on top of lots of much smaller scale dynamics, all the way down to the scale of atoms and eventually nuclei and elementary particles and all that other stuff.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So there's some quantum stuff that's going on that we describe as having a classical hardware level of bit exchange.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And then we describe the behavior of programs on top of that.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So what we want, what makes a computer useful is that we can assign semantics to programs, and we can talk about semantic relationships between programs.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: For example, the relationship between the Internet protocol stuff that Zoom is doing and what you actually see on your user interface and hear on your user interface that needs to stay fixed over time.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Or Zoom becomes incomprehensible and not programmable and in fact, not even well defined as an algorithmic system.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And the same is true for the relationship between the operating system and the hardware description, or between the operating system and zoom as a program.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So computer science works in exactly this scale free way.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so, in a sense, scale free explanation is very familiar.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's exactly the kind of explanation that we have in computer science.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that's why I referred to the relationship between scales as one of implementation, because that's a term that we're familiar with from thinking about computers implementing programs.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So what are these theories?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: If we think in biological terms, we can think of pathways being embedded in a cell, or cells being embedded in tissues, all the way up to niches of various Kinds, which may be social niches being embedded in ecosystems, and ecosystems being embedded in the biosphere.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so we have all of these essentially semantic theories that talk about how one scale embeds in another scale.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And if we have these sorts of scale transitions, we can think of representing the relationship between transitions at different scales in terms of the activity of some kind of renormalization group, which is transforming entities and processes at one scale into entities and processes at another scale.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And I think in ontology, we can at least put forward the hypothesis that all the way from pathways embedding in cells to ecosystems embedding in the biosphere, we could put forward the hypothesis, at least, that the renormalization group flow across all of these scales is trivial.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: That is that the embedding theories all have the same formal structure, that the structure that describes how pathways embed into cells is the same structure that describes how ecosystems embed into the biosphere.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Now, I certainly can't prove that.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: I believe that it's likely.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So I think it's an interesting hypothesis to investigate.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And this is an hypothesis that I want to leave you with as a result of this class is something to think about.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: To what extent, in thinking about biological systems or even social systems, are the embedding theories the same?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So, in thinking this way, that the physics of the situation has the same formal structure as computer science has in terms of explanation, we're of course, faced with a problem, which is that we're not just reconstructing physics, we're talking about the physics of interacting observers.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We're talking about the physics of communication.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we're modeling how we do physics.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that makes our theory self referential.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so we have to face the music from Goethel's theorem, which tells us essentially that powerful self referential theories can't be both consistent and complete.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And by powerful I just mean powerful enough to express arithmetic.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So not terribly powerful.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this becomes an issue that we have to live with.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We will always be faced with this issue of having to construct meta theories which tell us how our lower level theories work, but we never get to the end of that process.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We never can get to theories that are both consistent and complete, because our tower of theories becomes progressively, actually more powerful as it goes.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So Goethel, in a sense, poses a problem, but in another sense just tells us what life is like as a scientist, that you can't have everything all the time doing science, but we probably all already knew that.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So let's now talk about space, end of digression, and see how these ideas apply to a system or a tower of systems that can construct a spatial embedding in its world, in its observed world.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So let's start out thinking about a system that can see its environment, but what it sees is a completely uniform environment where nothing is happening.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if you have a uniform environment where nothing is happening, you can't distinguish one part of the environment from another from another.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: You have no sense of space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So what I want to do is build up from scratch what's needed to have a sense of space, and then we'll talk a little bit about what organisms are doing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And I think a very interesting question is, if you look at phylogeny, at what points in phylogeny, what lineages in phylogeny actually need to have a sense of space, and what do they have to have in terms of computational power to have that sense of space?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if you just have a uniform environment, you don't have a sense of space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But the first thing we can do with an environment is to divide it up into some number of parts that are somehow distinguishable.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So suppose we can segment the environment into two different parts.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And if you think about E.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Coli, for example, E.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Coli has a bunch of sensors on the front and a bunch of effectors on the back, so it can sense much more about the front part of the environment than the back part of the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So already with E.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Coli, you have this kind of segmentation of the environment into parts, but so far, nothing is happening in this environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We just have segments that can be distinguished.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So let's consider an environment like this, that has distinguishable segments.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: What one next wants to know about these segments is whether they're next to each other.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And if we just have a bunch of segments, we just have a set, and a set doesn't have any order or any relationship information.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So I've drawn this environment as a rectangle of rectangles, but that's just a representation.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And it looks like there are relationships between these rectangles, but if they're just a set, then there are no relationships.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: If we want to add relationships, then we have to add them explicitly.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So let's add some connections between these different segments of the environment to turn that set into a graph that says explicitly, for example, that the light green segment is attached to the light blue segment, and it's also attached to the dark green segment, and the dark blue segment is attached to the light blue segment and attached to the dark green segment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So now we have something that's much more mathematically complicated than a set.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have a graph that has some connection information.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we have a connection topological.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Now, adding this topology does something very important.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It breaks the exchange symmetry that is there if you just have a set.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if we just have a set, it doesn't make any difference if I exchange, for example, the positions of the upper right light blue segment with the upper left light green segment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But if we have this connection topology, then it does make a difference.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Right, I've twisted the graph around, and if I have to break connections to exchange things, then I've actually changed the topology.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So adding a topology, adding connections, can disrupt a symmetry that's there if there is no topology.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So now let's think about, now we have the structure that's required to think about something happening.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So suppose that at some time, as measured in the bit counter time reference frame of the observing system, something happens.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So a dot appears in the light green segment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we can express this actually in the notation of quantum field theory.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We can think of the light green segment as a field and the dot appearing is the occurrence of an excitation in that field.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so we can write this notation that says that the green field was excited to produce a dot which is up arrow Green dot.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And sometime after that it may turn out that the dot disappears in the green field and some sort of dot appears down in the dark blue field.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And again, we can write this in this kind of creation and destruction operator notation that one has in quantum field theory.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so this says that the green field is no longer excited, but now the dark blue field is excited.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this doesn't imply anything about these excitations being the same.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: In fact, they're completely different.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: One is an excitation of the green field and one is an excitation of the blue field.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But at least now something is happening in the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we can think about what does it take for an observer to notice that something is happening in its environment?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It has to be able to detect a change occurring in some segment of its environment, and that change can involve something happening or something stopping happening in that segment of its environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But it doesn't yet have to have any idea of what an object is.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But we can add that if the system has a memory, we can have the system connect these events happening in different parts of its environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if the system has a memory that has some number of steps, I'll say n steps, but here it could even just be two steps.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It can see transitions between these two different states, where there's a dot in the green field and then a dot in the dark blue field, and then a dot in the green field, and then a dot in the dark blue field, and then a dot in the green field, et cetera.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So I've expressed this in this sort of field theory notation over on the right side.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And what this is is a flip flop.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's an observed periodic behavior.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this is the basic idea behind a clock.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So any observer that can see this number of time steps internally can interpret what's going on in its external environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: As a clock ticking.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It can see some aperiodic.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So as long as you can have memory and the ability to detect change, you can see periodic behavior in the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So you can see the environment acting like a clock.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So let's think a bit about what this does and does not require.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So, seeing a clock in the environment requires having distinguishable, non exchangeable sectors of the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So you have to have this connection topology that breaks the exchange symmetry.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It requires having these sectors implement some sort of flip flop.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So something aperiodic happening, and you have to have enough memory to see that periodicity, but it doesn't require any sense of object identity.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So the excitation in the green part and the excitation in the blue part can still just be field excitations of the green part and the blue part.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: There's nothing that says that those have to be the same thing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: They just have to appear and disappear in some periodic way.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And having clock doesn't require a metric space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: You don't need to have any sense of distance defined on the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: You just have to have this segmentation that is not rearrangeable.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this tells us something extremely important, which is that time is more fundamental than space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Time in the exterior environment is much simpler and easier to observe than space in the exterior environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if we're thinking biologically about phylogeny, we might expect to see organisms that can detect periodic behavior in the external environment long before they can detect spatial organization in the exterior environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we know that organisms, even down to microbial mats, can respond to the diurnal cycle.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we know that organisms, in a sense, can detect environmental clocks, even organisms that we have no reason to believe, divide the environment up into spaces or the sort of space that we're used to, like a Euclidean space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So adding space to this Idea of time in the Environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So the Next step is to be able to see motion and being Able to see one thing move from one segment of the Environment to another segment, as opposed to something happening in One segment, and then something happens in another segment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: One has to have this idea of object persistence, that there's a thing that has an Identity, and Its identity doesn't change over time, and it doesn't change when you move it someplace else.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: When it appears someplace else in the Environment, it's the same object.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this is an idea that psychologists call object persistence, and it's an idea that physicists call translational invariance.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Translational invariance means two things.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It means that if I have an object and I move it to a different location, I don't change the object.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's the Same object that I move from here to there.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So the location doesn't change the object.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And it also means the reverse of that.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It means that the object doesn't change the location.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: My container remains invariant Even though I move the object around in it.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So these are kind of the two phases of translational invariance, and they're the two faces of object persistence.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: As the object moves through time, Its identity remains fixed, and it doesn't Change the time that it's moving through.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if I'm measuring Its Motion With a clock, moving the object doesn't Change the clock.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: These are clearly very classical ideas.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we talked about earlier Classical communication.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And when we talked about classical communication in, for Example, the context of a Bell EPR experiment, we talked about the observers being able to write down some data on a piece of paper or on a Disk drive or something and hand those Data to someone Else.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this is Translational Invariance.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: The Data Can't Change When Alice Gives it to Bob.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Otherwise, there isn't Classical Communication taking Place.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And of course, there's an up to noise built into here, right?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: The piece of paper might get wet and the ink might run a little bit, but it's still the same message.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: There's still some identity being assumed.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So object persistence is not an idea we get from quantum theory.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's an idea that we impose on top of quantum theory.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And it's this idea that's intrinsically classical.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we're looking right here at the quantum to classical transition.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: This is it.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: This is what gets added to quantum theory to get classical physics.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's this idea of object persistence.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Now, once we have object persistence, we can kind of go to town constructing space, and here's how we do it.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We all learned about object persistence this way when we were six months old, doing motor babbling and observing our hands and feeling how our bodies worked and seeing objects that we could manipulate and that didn't change when we manipulated them.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this is the birth of object persistence.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: This is the birth of classicality in human psychology.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So now let's start thinking about building a coordinate system.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: What's a coordinate system?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: A coordinate system is just a set of labels that are attached to these segments of the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And to build a coordinate system, you have to have an origin.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And an origin means an object, something that's fixed, something that doesn't move around.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so a coordinate system requires the ability to identify.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: A stigmergic memory requires the ability to find something in the environment that has a meaning that stays constant over time.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that's what a stigmergic memory is.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's something in the environment that provides us with a memory resource that we can count on being the same.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And it's having this fixed point that allows us to label these connected segments of the environment that contain objects that move and be able to say, okay, the object moved from this part of the Environment to another part, and I can give those parts labels with respect to this other part that doesn't move, this origin point.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And once I have this, I can construct other invariances.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So, for example, I can consider an object that rotates around this origin without changing its identity, and that defines what's called rotational invariance.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And I can also talk about an object that gets bigger and smaller compared to this fixed point and that defines radial distance.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And if you think about the baby in the previous slide that's doing motor babbling, it sees things getting smaller as it moves them farther away so the visual system does this computation for us and constructs this radial coordinate for us with respect to our bodies, or specifically our heads, our eyes.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So in doing this very early motor activity, we're actually building the spatial coordinate system for our brains that's implemented by the hippocampus, the place cells in the hippocampus.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And if I have an origin point in the environment, I can also infer that I am moving, that I have changed my location with respect to that object.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that's a considerably more complicated inference, because you have to have a representation of the self of you to say, I moved.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: You have to be able to locate, in a sense, metacognitively, a particular object that's you in that coordinate system.

sentences.text: So we're going to set that aside and now talk about adding some numbers.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So, adding a metric, and adding a metric requires another particular kind of object, which is a ruler, a particular fixed object that can be moved around and that has translational invariance, and translational invariance up to some transformation, up to some tensor.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And in Euclidean space, that tensor is the identity.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So in Euclidean space, you have perfect translational and rotational invariance.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: As you get into general relativity, then the ruler can actually change its length as you rotate, or the ruler can change its length as it moves through space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So effectively, your Spacetime can deform, the coordinates of your Spacetime can deform, and that gives you the representation of mass, of cOurse, in general relativity.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we talked several sessions ago about quantum reference frames, and I used the example of rulers and clocks as quantum reference frames.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So now we see how to construct those from observations and symmetry breaking and object identity, all of which we need to define a quantum reference frame out in the environment, like a ruler.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And notice that we don't need any of that environmental stuff to define those QRFs within our own processing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And in fact, the ones that exist within us, we have no direct access to.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We can look at someone else's brain and talk about their spatial representation system, but we can't look inside our own brains and talk about our spatial representation system.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this is how we get a metric space from the ground up.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we've talked about this from a very psychological or biological point of view, starting from sort of motor capabilities, motor babbling, for example, a measure of effort which gives you some sense of mass.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So if it's easy to move something, it's light, and if it's hard to move something, it's heavy.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we understand that when we're six months old, because we can measure how much force we're having to apply with our muscles.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have a reference internally for this force that we're applying, and we use that internal measurement to attribute this idea of mass to things in the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have to have memory from manipulations.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have to be able to identify invariances that define objects object persistence.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we have to be able to build a ruler that we can move around and use to define a metric space.

sentences.text: Now, this is very different from the way physicists approach this.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: If you look at the physics literature, then people start with information transfer.

sentences.text: And the most well known one is the duality between antidicitter space, which is the sort of space you see inside a black hole, and conformal field theory, a quantum field theory on the boundary of the black hole.

sentences.text: So things you can see, for example, going on, on the horizon of a black hole are dual to the geometry and the interior.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: By this mathematical Relationship, you can use that mathematical relationship to construct quantum error correcting code.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Code by using the symmetries of the field theory as a resource for redundancy that allows you to represent the same thing in different places.

sentences.text: And as soon as you can do that, you can build up a network of elements that look basically like elements of a lattice.

sentences.text: And a lattice is a graph to which you can assign symmetric relationships, and you get a metric space.

sentences.text: And in physics, typically, the goal is to get Einstein's equations out of this to start with some information, theoretic sorts of constructs, and get the equations of general relativity.

sentences.text: But what are the equations of general mean?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: These are things that Einstein derived by doing fairly simple thought experiments, using the invariances of ordinary Euclidean space, combined with ideas from special relativity about the speed of light being constant.

sentences.text: And he added the principle of equivalence, which is the idea that essentially mass and acceleration are the same thing, or that gravity and acceleration are the same, that weight and acceleration are the same thing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So it's at least reasonable to expect that this inferential process that's going on in theoretical physics is generating the same thing, although in a very formalized way that we can generate by thinking about how organisms deal with their environments.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And so I want to leave this with you as the second hypothesis here.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: The first one was the hypothesis about a trivial renormalization group flow across scales and biology.

sentences.text: The second hypothesis is that these two approaches to emergent Spacetime are actually giving us the same information.

sentences.text: And maybe starting out with the same information, in fact, that we may be able to think about these fundamental building blocks of information flow and entanglement.

sentences.text: In terms of the sorts of perceptual relationships that we've been talking about in this class.

sentences.text: So there's our second hypothesis to think about going forward.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And I just want to leave you with the idea that organisms at least manage this very interesting process that we can think of starting as starting with the construct of memory.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Organisms have memory at multiple scales, and it's memory that allows them to formulate the idea that there are objects.

sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So you can do error correction.

sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Code.

sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So you can build libraries, or you can build computers, or you can build the Internet, if you have Spacetime, which gives you more memory, which gives you more object persistence, which gives you more error correction.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And the circle just spins around.
sentences.speaker: A

I mean, here the time span is three and a half or 4 billion years between us and LUCA. These lineages have been diverging for that long, but they're still continuous. And in particular, they form a continuous cell membrane. So when you think of life in this way, we realize that we are reasoning from just one example when we think about terrestrial life. And this strongly limits what we can say about living systems, what we can say about biology, that we really only have one example, the lineage that descends from LUCA here on Earth. And at some point, we may have more examples. And there's certainly groups working on artificial organisms that aren't part of this Lineage, that are constructed from parts derived from this Lineage, but aren't members of this Lineage themselves. And that may tell us something new about life. But if we think of life this way, we see something very important, which is that as life Grows, its boundary gets bigger. And since the boundary of a system constitutes its informational environment, its dimension getting bigger means that more information flows into it from its environment and more information flows out of it into its environment. So as life develops from LUCA, it gets a larger and larger informational environment, and this dimension of its boundary grows and grows. Now, what that means, if you go back to our original picture of two interacting systems, is that the dimensionality of the physical environment is decreasing. And we think of the physical environment as increasing in size. We have the expanding universe and all that. But what's increasing in size is space. And if space is emergent, then that increase is not a real increase in degrees of freedom. What we're really interested in is the Hilbert Space of the physical environment, as distinct from the Hilbert space of life. And as life gets bigger, it literally qubits, literally eats the physical environment and turns it into more life. So there's less physical environment around. So the trajectory of life is toward a bigger informational environment and a smaller physical environment. And as the physical environment gets smaller, you might imagine it gets easier to predict. And as the Informational environment gets bigger, you have more information with which to predict the behavior of the physical environment. So this all hangs together very nicely with the free energy principle. Here's another picture of this same thing. If we start with some boundary here on the left labeled B, around some system labeled S, and it's embedded in an environment, E. Then as S makes copies of itself through some process like cell division, then it starts to fill up more of E, it's actually converting degrees of freedom of E into degrees of freedom of its copies that it's made of itself. And if we think of some larger boundary drawn somewhere in E, here on the right side, I've labeled that B prime. What happens is that B prime gets slowly filled up with copies of S, and it starts to look like a large organism. And that's what life is doing in the physical environment. It's making a bigger boundary for itself at the expense of degrees of freedom of its physical environment. So we can ask, what drives this process? Why is life doing this? Why is it making copies of itself? And the answer to that question, at least one answer to that question, is the free energy principle drives it to do this. And I'll just show you some simulations from several years ago of a cell population. In this upper left panel, the green cells are stem cells that divide, and they've been embedded in an environment that's safe on the left side and 100% lethal on the right side. So they're embedded in an environment that's conducive to life on one side and very dangerous as you get toward the middle. And the purpose of these simulations was to study what happens when the stem cells are able to divide and create not just other stem cells, but create specialized progeny that don't divide. So somatic progeny that don't divide and hence have free energy resources, thermodynamic resources, that they can devote to doing something other than dividing. Cell division is incredibly expensive when it comes to energy. So if you take that energy and apply it not to cell division, but to protecting the stem cells, you can allow the stem cell population to expand. And that's what these other simulations show. The blue cells are somatic cells that have very varying ability to protect the stem cells. And if they're fairly good at protection and they're fairly hard to kill, down in the right bottom Quadrant, you can actually get a population expanding well into the highly lethal part of the environment. So this shows you the FEP in action. What the stem cells are doing is constructing a very predictable neighborhood around themselves in the environment by dividing to make progeny that don't themselves divide, that just sit there and help protect the stem cells. So the stem cells are now living in a safer, more predictable environment, and that allows them to invade more and more of their physical environment by having this fairly benign, informational environment. So this is the FEP in action driving the expansion of life at the expense of the physical environment. So that lets us go back to this question that was raised last time about the mechanism of these scale transitions that we see ubiquitously in life. Life gets bigger and bigger as time goes on phytogenetically and as time goes on developmentally, we start with some molecular pathways that somehow get assembled into a cell. That's the origin of life question, how does that happen? And about 2 billion years later, cells start to group together to make multicellular organisms. Now, bacteria group together to make facultative multicellular systems like microbial maps. 3 billion years ago, very, very early on. But we don't see the emergence of obligate multicellulars until much, much later, before the Cambrian explosion, but still less than a billion years ago. And from there, things get more complicated very quickly. So one has large multicellular organisms. They develop complicated social relations that probably first emerged with social insects, but are certainly well developed in invertebrates, including in mammals. Organisms group together in very complex ecosystems. And recall here that it's now known that all multicellular organisms have obligate microbial symbiotes. So all of our bodies are, in fact, very complex ecosystems populated by many, many different species of bacteria. And that's true not just for us, but for trees and insects and worms and sponges and everything else. So organisms, from a body point of view, are themselves ecosystems. And organisms organize themselves into ecosystems, and these ecosystems come into contact across the entire biosphere. So processes as simple as the wind disperse organisms as small as bacteria all over the planet. So this scaling of life toward larger and larger organizational structures is, in a sense, the major thing for biology to explain. And the hypothesis that we floated last time was that this transition from very small scales to very large scales uses the same mechanism over and over again, or a mechanism that has the same structure over and over again. So the renormalization group is trivial. Basically, it's just the identity operating at different scales or mapping from one scale to the next. So the question is, can we approach this in any way? Does this make sense? And to try to make sense of it, we can go to the R1 developed theory that we have in biology, which has been formulated by Dawkins and others as universal Darwinism. This is just kind of an abstraction of the modern synthesis between Darwinian evolution and genetics. But universal Darwinism is incredibly simple and very obvious. It says if you have systems and they can copy each other, they can copy themselves, and the copies can diversify. Then if you want to know what's going to happen at the population level, what you will find is the systems that copy themselves and diversify most efficiently will win because there'll be more of them, so they end up dominating the population, and winning gets called natural selection. But natural selection is not an extra part of the Darwinian process. It's just the outcome of efficiency of the systems that copy themselves most efficiently, coming to dominate any population. So there's no sort of kind of hand of god or whatever, reaching down and selecting some organisms and not others. And of course, when Darwin put the idea of natural selection together, he was thinking very explicitly of the analogy of a gardener or a farmer selecting the crops or the animals or whatever that the gardener liked best, and keeping those. And that's where this selection metaphor comes from. But there's no real process of selection in evolution by natural selection. It's just copying and diversifying. But this clearly is just the outline of what a real mechanistic theory would be, because we need to have a story about what copying is and what diversifying is and what efficiently means. And in particular, to address the question that we raised a couple of slides ago, we need to know whether these mechanisms are the same, or at least isomorphic, of the same form at different scales. So that's what I want to talk about for the next little bit. Let's start with copying. Up until the 70s, copying in biology really meant DNA replication and, to some extent, cell division. But the focus in evolutionary theory was on DNA replication. And in the 70s, it was realized that whole genes could be duplicated, so whole genes could be copied. And then shortly after that, it was realized that particularly in prokaryotes, where genes, functionally related genes are next to each other in chromosomes, often in what are called operons, that operons could be duplicated and so entire pathways could be duplicated. And as genomes began to be sequenced and structures of genomes were understood, it became clear that genomes could be copied. And of course, we have two copies in each of our cells, with the exception of red blood cells of our complete genome. But some plants, for example, have six or eight or even more copies of their genome in each of their cells. So there's large scale genome duplication. Cell division is clonal duplication of cells. Organismal reproduction works by cell division. In all known systems, colonies or societies of organisms reproduce themselves, in part through cultural transmission, and entire niches reproduce themselves, for example, in processes like forest evolution or desertification, or even urbanizaTion. We see humans reproducing the same sorts of niches in city after city, for example. So these forms of copying have the kind of hierarchical dependencies that one might expect. So to duplicate pathways, you have to duplicate genes. To duplicate cells, you have to duplicate the genome. To duplicate organisms, you have to duplicate cells. And this suggests that this copying operation is indeed scale free, that the copying operation at each level enables the copying operation at the next level. Now, with diversification, we see much the same thing in the early days of the modern synthesis and still in the work of people like Richard Dawkins. Diversification is generally thought of as random. So mutation, for example, is thought of as random. And here I have Barbara McClintock, who is kind of the hero of non randomness in doggedly over decades, pointing out that much of genome diversification is not random at all, and that genomes actively diversify by moving whole clusters of genes around and duplicating them, or just changing their positions so that they're under the influence of different local control. So at the gene and genome level, you have active diversification by various processes, enzymatic processes. As McClintock showed us, transposon mediated mechanisms, which are enzymatic. At the bottom, cells actively diversify by lots of different mechanisms. And in the 70s, Carl Woes was in part large, personally responsible for pointing out that in the microbial world there's a lot of gene transfer. And again, no one believed him for quite a while. But now it's broadly accepted that microbes exchange DNA very frequently and across large distances phylogenetically. And this is how things like microbial resistance to antibiotics spread so quickly, or one way that it spreads so quickly. And it's a tremendous agent of essentially speciation to the extent that that even makes any sense in the microbial world. Of course, in our cells we have functional differentiation. As mentioned earlier, there are lots of symbiotic interactions that lead to diversification in cells by radically altering their local environments. And of course, sex is a mechanism for diversification. Organisms actively diversify in many different ways. The most obvious one is just by moving around, by moving to a different environment, the organism is exposed to different inputs and is allowed different outputs, and so it can move into a different direction, morphologically, genetically, et cetera. Organisms can regulate their own evolvability by altering things like DNA repair systems or activating transposons. Again, these are sorts of things that went very much against the grain when they were first discovered, but are now pretty well accepted. And of course, urorganism can learn and so can diversify their behavior by diversifying their computational capabilities. And social groups, of course, actively diversify in many different ways. And organisms are increasingly, non human organisms are increasingly regarded as having cultures that they pass on intergenerationally by intergenerational learning and can exchange with other groups. So diversification is active and occurs at every scale. And, again, diversity, although this is a bit less clear than in the case of copying. Diversification mechanisms at one scale enable diversification mechanisms at other scales. So, for example, transpose, unmediated mechanisms enable horizontal gene transfer in microorganisms. And the FEP tells us that efficiency is actually about intelligence, because the FEP drives systems to build good models of their environments or the behavior of their environments. And what a good model lets a system do is reach a single goal by many different means, because it allows, in a sense, planning, and it allows flexibility and adaptability. And I put William James here on this slide because he was the first, as far as I know, to define intelligence as this ability to use different means to reach the same goal. Now, in evolution, that's long been known, and it's called convergent evolution, when you see two lineages adapting to a single environment with very different genetics and very different morphologies, and often the organisms will end up with similar morphologies that work well in that environment, but very different genetics and very different biochemistry. So throughout evolution, we see this phenomenon of functional convergence, balancing structural divergence at many, many different levels. So we have multiple genes for very similar proteins. We have multiple pathways that do more or less the same thing. We have different cell types that support the same basic functions. We have tissues that are fairly different, but that have the same functions, for example, eyes and different kinds of organisms that allow vision, but have very different structure. And, of course, we have functional convergence and social relations. And if we look at how cells interact, traditional evolutionary theory really focuses on competition. But we now know that cells cooperate, that they exchange resources in various ways, even across vast differences in phylogeny, for example, the interchange between plants and fungi, or between bacteria and us. We know that cells, in a sense, persuade each other by secreting things like hormones, that cause other cells to do different things. Cells deceive each other, for example, microbes that are trying to escape the immune system, and cells coerce each other. Cells even kill each other when they detect, for example, genetic defects. So these sorts of social and economic and even political ideas are useful for describing living systems from the level of cells on up. They were developed in social settings to describe what goes on in human societies and then extended to other animals. And now it's very clear that they extend to individual cells. So when we think about social intelligence. We can think about social intelligence even at the level of individual cells. And we see these sorts of competition, cooperation, resource exchange, et cetera, even at the level of microbial mats. So, biological structures that are 3 billion years old. Now, of course, intelligence is necessary, but it's not sufficient for being selected. It won't protect you from impacts of asteroids that happen to land on your planet, which has happened often in the evolution of the Earth. And we're now trying to figure out how to predict and prevent such things. But who knows whether we'll be successful at that? But this intelligence is necessary when it's viewed in this FEP sort of way. Intelligence is what lets you build models that enable you to predict the environment. So where does this leave us? By thinking of evolutionary theory in terms of scale free mechanisms, we seem to have a picture in which we start with quantum systems with a certain level of complexity, and the FEP actually gives us scale free biology, or something very close to scale free biology. And that's very interesting, because the FEP, of course, is a generic principle. It just says that systems do what they need to do to keep existing. And this way of thinking gives us some predictions. One is that we'll find compartmentalized problem solving everywhere, because the FEP drives compartmentalization. And the reason is just non commutativity of measurement processes. It predicts that we'll see hierarchical organization everywhere, in the same way we did on that first compartmentalization slide, where once you have a number of compartments, you need a metacompartment that, if nothing else, distributes free energy. So some sort of very basic attention system. And we see attention systems, of course, throughout biology. It predicts that living systems will have very limited classical data structures. So since they have to write classical data on their boundaries, and their boundaries are much smaller than they are, and because writing classical data is expensive, the living systems will tend to use as little classical data as they can get away with, since classical data is needed for thermodynamic irreversibility, where we see thermodynamic irreversibility, that's where we look for classical data. We saw that organisms will be able to detect time first before they can detect space. So we can expect organisms to have clocks even before they can represent space. And, of course, we see things like diurnal variation throughout biology. And finally, the FEP predicts this asymptotic collapse of separability back to entanglement. So it predicts that living systems will eventually degrade and become indistinguishable from their environments. And we know that happens at the cell level and the individual organism level. We call it death. So the FEP seems to give us a lot of the features of biology, and it gives us these features in a scale free way, and it derives them from this very basic physics. So where does that leave us? I think it leaves us here with a challenge not just to thinking about the FEP, which is what this course has been about, but to quantum information theory in general. And that challenge is to evolve from the kind of contextuality and theoretical utility that we've been discussing in this course, and which is very well developed in the physics community, to some sorts of empirical and topological utility. And I've listed three areas here where QIt is very active, one in quantum gravity and cosmology. And you're probably familiar with things like string theory that sort of fairly famously seem not to be empirically testable. And the quantum gravity community is enormous, many thousands of people working in this area. But coming up with theories that can be tested empirically at the scales that we can actually do experiments, so at accessible energy scales, for example, has proved to be very difficult. So this is a real challenge to the field, is somehow getting not just to empirical testability, but to some sort of technological utility. And you can imagine that if the. If the main prediction of quantum gravity is that Spacetime is emergent, that there could be enormous utility in that some ability to manipulate the way Spacetime emerges. The second area, of course, is quantum information and computing. And here massive resources are being put into technological utility. And I think it's reasonable to expect that we'll have useful quantum computers within a generation, at any rate. So there, I think the field is going quite well. And the last area, what we've talked about here, is quantum biochemistry and biology. And this, I think, is an area with enormous practice promise that maybe some of you will actually contribute to making this area more useful topological and more accessible empirically. But at least we have a picture of how these different areas fit together. So that's it. Thank you very much for participating in this class. Andrew will be doing your questions.

Thank you, Daniel. And welcome, everyone, to this last session that I'll be doing with a focus on biology. And just to give a brief review. As usual, we've focused in this course on generic quantum systems, by which I mean just any quantum system that has some number of degrees of freedom. And we really haven't made any assumptions about these systems other than the assumption that both interacting partners have sufficient degrees of freedom that they can be considered separable.

So their boundary is small with respect to the total size of each of the interacting systems. And I want to emphasize again that the approach we've taken is completely topological. So we haven't assumed anything about embedding in space. And as we've characterized these systems, we focused really on two things. One, the amount of information that the two systems can exchange.

And that amount is determined by the size of their boundary. It's determined by this number, n, which is the Hilbert Space dimension of the boundary. And as we've discussed now in several of the sessions, we can think of this boundary as a collection of N qubits via which the two systems, A and B, communicate. The other feature of the interaction on which we focused is the reference frames that are used by the two systems to interact with this set of qubits. And it's these reference frames that assign the information that flows between A and B, meaning or Functional significance or actionability, or however you want to refer to the idea that when a system gets some information, it does something useful with it.

sentences.text: It says if you have systems and they can copy each other, they can copy themselves, and the copies can diversify.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Then if you want to know what's going to happen at the population level, what you will find is the systems that copy themselves and diversify most efficiently will win because there'll be more of them, so they end up dominating the population, and winning gets called natural selection.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But natural selection is not an extra part of the Darwinian process.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's just the outcome of efficiency of the systems that copy themselves most efficiently, coming to dominate any population.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So there's no sort of kind of hand of god or whatever, reaching down and selecting some organisms and not others.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And of course, when Darwin put the idea of natural selection together, he was thinking very explicitly of the analogy of a gardener or a farmer selecting the crops or the animals or whatever that the gardener liked best, and keeping those.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that's where this selection metaphor comes from.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But there's no real process of selection in evolution by natural selection.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It's just copying and diversifying.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But this clearly is just the outline of what a real mechanistic theory would be, because we need to have a story about what copying is and what diversifying is and what efficiently means.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And in particular, to address the question that we raised a couple of slides ago, we need to know whether these mechanisms are the same, or at least isomorphic, of the same form at different scales.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So that's what I want to talk about for the next little bit.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Let's start with copying.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Up until the 70s, copying in biology really meant DNA replication and, to some extent, cell division.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But the focus in evolutionary theory was on DNA replication.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And in the 70s, it was realized that whole genes could be duplicated, so whole genes could be copied.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And then shortly after that, it was realized that particularly in prokaryotes, where genes, functionally related genes are next to each other in chromosomes, often in what are called operons, that operons could be duplicated and so entire pathways could be duplicated.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And as genomes began to be sequenced and structures of genomes were understood, it became clear that genomes could be copied.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And of course, we have two copies in each of our cells, with the exception of red blood cells of our complete genome.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But some plants, for example, have six or eight or even more copies of their genome in each of their cells.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So there's large scale genome duplication.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Cell division is clonal duplication of cells.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Organismal reproduction works by cell division.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: In all known systems, colonies or societies of organisms reproduce themselves, in part through cultural transmission, and entire niches reproduce themselves, for example, in processes like forest evolution or desertification, or even urbanizaTion.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We see humans reproducing the same sorts of niches in city after city, for example.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So these forms of copying have the kind of hierarchical dependencies that one might expect.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So to duplicate pathways, you have to duplicate genes.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: To duplicate cells, you have to duplicate the genome.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: To duplicate organisms, you have to duplicate cells.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And this suggests that this copying operation is indeed scale free, that the copying operation at each level enables the copying operation at the next level.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Now, with diversification, we see much the same thing in the early days of the modern synthesis and still in the work of people like Richard Dawkins.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Diversification is generally thought of as random.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So mutation, for example, is thought of as random.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And here I have Barbara McClintock, who is kind of the hero of non randomness in doggedly over decades, pointing out that much of genome diversification is not random at all, and that genomes actively diversify by moving whole clusters of genes around and duplicating them, or just changing their positions so that they're under the influence of different local control.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So at the gene and genome level, you have active diversification by various processes, enzymatic processes.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: As McClintock showed us, transposon mediated mechanisms, which are enzymatic.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: At the bottom, cells actively diversify by lots of different mechanisms.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And in the 70s, Carl Woes was in part large, personally responsible for pointing out that in the microbial world there's a lot of gene transfer.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And again, no one believed him for quite a while.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But now it's broadly accepted that microbes exchange DNA very frequently and across large distances phylogenetically.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And this is how things like microbial resistance to antibiotics spread so quickly, or one way that it spreads so quickly.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And it's a tremendous agent of essentially speciation to the extent that that even makes any sense in the microbial world.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Of course, in our cells we have functional differentiation.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: As mentioned earlier, there are lots of symbiotic interactions that lead to diversification in cells by radically altering their local environments.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And of course, sex is a mechanism for diversification.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Organisms actively diversify in many different ways.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: The most obvious one is just by moving around, by moving to a different environment, the organism is exposed to different inputs and is allowed different outputs, and so it can move into a different direction, morphologically, genetically, et cetera.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Organisms can regulate their own evolvability by altering things like DNA repair systems or activating transposons.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Again, these are sorts of things that went very much against the grain when they were first discovered, but are now pretty well accepted.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And of course, urorganism can learn and so can diversify their behavior by diversifying their computational capabilities.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And social groups, of course, actively diversify in many different ways.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And organisms are increasingly, non human organisms are increasingly regarded as having cultures that they pass on intergenerationally by intergenerational learning and can exchange with other groups.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So diversification is active and occurs at every scale.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And, again, diversity, although this is a bit less clear than in the case of copying.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Diversification mechanisms at one scale enable diversification mechanisms at other scales.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So, for example, transpose, unmediated mechanisms enable horizontal gene transfer in microorganisms.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And the FEP tells us that efficiency is actually about intelligence, because the FEP drives systems to build good models of their environments or the behavior of their environments.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And what a good model lets a system do is reach a single goal by many different means, because it allows, in a sense, planning, and it allows flexibility and adaptability.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And I put William James here on this slide because he was the first, as far as I know, to define intelligence as this ability to use different means to reach the same goal.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Now, in evolution, that's long been known, and it's called convergent evolution, when you see two lineages adapting to a single environment with very different genetics and very different morphologies, and often the organisms will end up with similar morphologies that work well in that environment, but very different genetics and very different biochemistry.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So throughout evolution, we see this phenomenon of functional convergence, balancing structural divergence at many, many different levels.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we have multiple genes for very similar proteins.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have multiple pathways that do more or less the same thing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have different cell types that support the same basic functions.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We have tissues that are fairly different, but that have the same functions, for example, eyes and different kinds of organisms that allow vision, but have very different structure.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And, of course, we have functional convergence and social relations.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And if we look at how cells interact, traditional evolutionary theory really focuses on competition.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But we now know that cells cooperate, that they exchange resources in various ways, even across vast differences in phylogeny, for example, the interchange between plants and fungi, or between bacteria and us.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We know that cells, in a sense, persuade each other by secreting things like hormones, that cause other cells to do different things.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Cells deceive each other, for example, microbes that are trying to escape the immune system, and cells coerce each other.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Cells even kill each other when they detect, for example, genetic defects.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So these sorts of social and economic and even political ideas are useful for describing living systems from the level of cells on up.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: They were developed in social settings to describe what goes on in human societies and then extended to other animals.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And now it's very clear that they extend to individual cells.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So when we think about social intelligence.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We can think about social intelligence even at the level of individual cells.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we see these sorts of competition, cooperation, resource exchange, et cetera, even at the level of microbial mats.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So, biological structures that are 3 billion years old.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Now, of course, intelligence is necessary, but it's not sufficient for being selected.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It won't protect you from impacts of asteroids that happen to land on your planet, which has happened often in the evolution of the Earth.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we're now trying to figure out how to predict and prevent such things.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But who knows whether we'll be successful at that?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But this intelligence is necessary when it's viewed in this FEP sort of way.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: Intelligence is what lets you build models that enable you to predict the environment.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So where does this leave us?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: By thinking of evolutionary theory in terms of scale free mechanisms, we seem to have a picture in which we start with quantum systems with a certain level of complexity, and the FEP actually gives us scale free biology, or something very close to scale free biology.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that's very interesting, because the FEP, of course, is a generic principle.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It just says that systems do what they need to do to keep existing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And this way of thinking gives us some predictions.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: One is that we'll find compartmentalized problem solving everywhere, because the FEP drives compartmentalization.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And the reason is just non commutativity of measurement processes.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It predicts that we'll see hierarchical organization everywhere, in the same way we did on that first compartmentalization slide, where once you have a number of compartments, you need a metacompartment that, if nothing else, distributes free energy.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So some sort of very basic attention system.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we see attention systems, of course, throughout biology.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: It predicts that living systems will have very limited classical data structures.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So since they have to write classical data on their boundaries, and their boundaries are much smaller than they are, and because writing classical data is expensive, the living systems will tend to use as little classical data as they can get away with, since classical data is needed for thermodynamic irreversibility, where we see thermodynamic irreversibility, that's where we look for classical data.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We saw that organisms will be able to detect time first before they can detect space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So we can expect organisms to have clocks even before they can represent space.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And, of course, we see things like diurnal variation throughout biology.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And finally, the FEP predicts this asymptotic collapse of separability back to entanglement.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So it predicts that living systems will eventually degrade and become indistinguishable from their environments.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And we know that happens at the cell level and the individual organism level.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: We call it death.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So the FEP seems to give us a lot of the features of biology, and it gives us these features in a scale free way, and it derives them from this very basic physics.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So where does that leave us?
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: I think it leaves us here with a challenge not just to thinking about the FEP, which is what this course has been about, but to quantum information theory in general.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And that challenge is to evolve from the kind of contextuality and theoretical utility that we've been discussing in this course, and which is very well developed in the physics community, to some sorts of empirical and topological utility.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And you're probably familiar with things like string theory that sort of fairly famously seem not to be empirically testable.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And the quantum gravity community is enormous, many thousands of people working in this area.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: But coming up with theories that can be tested empirically at the scales that we can actually do experiments, so at accessible energy scales, for example, has proved to be very difficult.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: So this is a real challenge to the field, is somehow getting not just to empirical testability, but to some sort of technological utility.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And you can imagine that if the.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: If the main prediction of quantum gravity is that Spacetime is emergent, that there could be enormous utility in that some ability to manipulate the way Spacetime emerges.

sentences.text: The second area, of course, is quantum information and computing.
sentences.speaker: A

sentences.text: And here massive resources are being put into technological utility.
